facts.text: A guide dog puppy goes to live with a volunteer foster family when it is about 2 months old.
The foster family spends about a year helping the puppy learn good habits and get used to life among people; the school pays for food and medical care.
Foster families keep the dogs until they are about one and a half years old; the dogs then go back for about one more year of training.
Raising a guide dog takes about three years in all, and only about 30 percent of the dogs finally qualify.
In 2024 guide dogs in training practiced staying calm among more than 10,000 cheering fans at a baseball game in the Taipei Dome.
Taiwan has about 60,000 visually impaired people but only around 50 working guide dogs.
The International Guide Dog Federation's ideal is one guide dog for every 100 visually impaired people, which would mean at least 600 dogs in Taiwan.
About 10 guide dogs are trained and matched with users in Taiwan each year.
Taiwan's first guide dog, a Labrador named Aggie, was trained in Japan for half a year and began working on November 1, 1996.
When Aggie first worked on the streets, buses sometimes refused to carry her and restaurants turned her away.
Aggie retired in 2003 after more than seven years of work and lived with an adoptive family until she died in 2011 at age 16.
Aggie's user, Ko Ming-chi, worked with her to change the rules so guide dogs could ride public transport and enter public places.
Taiwanese law lets qualified guide dogs, and puppies with their trainers, freely enter public places, shops, restaurants and public transport.
Under the law, owners of these places may not refuse a guide dog, charge extra for it or add other conditions.
The law also says people should not touch, feed or distract a working guide dog with sounds or hand signals.
A place that refuses a guide dog and does not correct the problem in time can be fined NT$10,000 to NT$50,000.
Working guide dogs wear a guide harness, and puppies in training wear a vest that says they are in training.
The health ministry recorded 47 reports of guide dogs being refused entry between 2023 and 2025; restaurants, hotels and taxi drivers often think they are pets.
Retired guide dogs are adopted by families; in 2016 President Tsai Ing-wen adopted three retired guide dogs, and about five or six retire each year.
The training school must take proper care of guide dogs that retire or stop working and may not abandon them.
